United States: prices rise 0.4% in October, more than expected, and the Fed prepares a rate hike in December

On Tuesday, November 10, US inflation for October came in above expectations: +0.4% over the month, and +0.3% excluding energy and food, for the third month in a row. Fed Governor Christopher Waller backs a rate hike in December, and Wall Street fell [1][2][3][4].

According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), the consumer price index rose 0.4% in October, seasonally adjusted. Excluding food and energy ("core" inflation), it gained 0.3%, as in September and August [2]. Both figures beat forecasts [1][3].

In detail, energy rose 0.7% over the month, after a 5.2% jump in September; gasoline gained 1% and is still up 37.4% over a year [2]. Food rose 0.5%, and shelter 0.3%, which accounts for more than 30% of the month's total increase [2].

The annual figure is missing: the BLS did not collect prices in October 2025, during the federal government shutdown, and so cannot publish the 12-month change [2]. According to CNN, the annual pace is around 4% [7].

The same day, Christopher Waller, a governor of the Federal Reserve (Fed), said he would support a quarter-point (0.25 point) rate hike at the December 8-9 meeting, and that a larger hike should be considered if inflation stayed high [3]. According to CNBC, he opens the door to a half point [4].
In the government bond market, the 10-year yield returned to 5%, and the 2-year yield rose 0.17 point, its biggest one-day increase since April 2025 [6].
At the close, the Dow Jones lost 0.30% to 52,231.89 points, the S&P 500 0.38% to 7,520.93 points and the Nasdaq 0.74% to 25,065.87 points [3].
Nvidia fell 5.47%, its second session of losses, weighed down by the affair involving its CEO Jensen Huang [5].

Key takeaway: US inflation is not coming down, and the Fed is getting ready to raise rates again. Three months in a row at +0.3% excluding energy and food is a sign that price increases are spreading beyond gasoline, and it is exactly the threshold Christopher Waller was watching to consider a larger hike [2][4].

The mechanism: when prices rise faster than expected, investors anticipate higher rates. Government bond yields climb, which makes credit more expensive and weighs on stocks, especially tech stocks whose value rests on future profits [3][6].
The rise in energy remains at the heart of the problem: with gasoline up 37.4% over a year, the war around the Strait of Hormuz shows up in US prices, then in rents and food [2].

For you in France, a Fed that raises rates tends to strengthen the dollar against the euro, which makes oil paid in dollars and trips to the United States more expensive. Savings invested in US stocks may also be shaken between now and December.

According to the Times of Israel, Benjamin Netanyahu is reportedly calling Trump every day to push him to resume the war [9].

Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin said Qatar would host Vice President JD Vance and Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, next week; according to him, the disagreement is over who will take the first step [1].

What is new: the possible Vance-Rezaei meeting in Qatar, revealed by Turkey then denied by Iran, and Trump's calmer tone, as he is in no hurry to resume strikes as long as the blockade holds [1][2].

For you in France, Brent below 90 dollars, even for a moment, is good news for fuel prices. But as long as tankers are being targeted and no meeting is confirmed, this easing remains fragile.

On Tuesday, November 10, Russians, Ukrainians and Americans talked for nearly four hours in Abu Dhabi. Kyiv calls the day "constructive", Washington "very productive". A large prisoner swap was discussed, but Moscow wants a new European security order to be the core of the talks [1][2].
These three-way talks, the first since February, lasted nearly four hours; a second session was scheduled for Wednesday, November 11 [1][2].

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called the day "constructive and quite substantive" [1]. From Paris, where he was attending a G7 meeting, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio described the talks as "very productive", while urging patience [1].

According to a senior Ukrainian official, the two sides discussed a large-scale prisoner exchange, with details to be discussed in the coming days [1]. Zelensky said the talks were mainly about humanitarian issues: prisoners, detained Ukrainian civilians and children taken out of the country [6].
The head of the Ukrainian delegation, Rustem Umerov, cites four priorities: ending hostilities, reliable post-war security guarantees, rebuilding the economy and humanitarian measures [6].

On the Russian side, the 11-member delegation is led by Kremlin aide Vladimir Medinsky, with two deputy foreign ministers and military and intelligence officials [2]. A source in this delegation told Reuters that Moscow sees a new security architecture for Europe as the main purpose of the talks, with Ukraine being only "one aspect" [2][5].

Russia refuses to have the Europeans at the table, while saying the European Union could join later [1]. Representatives of France, the United Kingdom, Germany, Italy, the EU and NATO were expected in Abu Dhabi to talk with the Americans and Ukrainians [2]. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas replied: "We already have a European security architecture in place" [2].

According to a US official quoted by Reuters, envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner could then travel to Russia to meet Vladimir Putin [4]. A few days earlier, an overnight Russian attack targeted Kyiv with 36 ballistic missiles, according to Zelensky, and hit a substation linking two nuclear plants to the capital [7].
Key takeaway: the tone is positive, but positions have not moved. The two governments remain far apart on the key points of a deal, and analysts were not expecting a breakthrough [1][3].

The Russian demand changes the scale: by putting the security of all of Europe at the center, Moscow turns Ukraine into a mere part of a broader negotiation about the continent. The Europeans reply that these issues can only be discussed after the war ends [2].
The prisoner swap is the most concrete short-term result: it is often the first possible gesture between two countries at war, before any ceasefire [1].

For you in France, these talks matter twice over: Paris is one of the European capitals Moscow wants to keep out, and a real peace would affect energy prices and European defense budgets, which have been climbing since 2022.

Key takeaway: 67 recommendations do not make a coalition. Eisenkot has a majority on paper, not yet a government, because many parties refuse to sit with others [4][8].

AI: Microsoft asks Trump not to ban a key Chinese part of its data centers

According to Reuters, Microsoft is pressing the Trump administration to drop a ban on new models of Chinese optical transceivers, parts that move data around artificial intelligence data centers. Washington fears espionage; Microsoft fears slowing down its construction projects [1][2].

According to three people familiar with the matter quoted by Reuters on November 10, Microsoft is pushing the Trump administration to abandon its plan to bar imports of new models of Chinese optical transceivers [1][2]. Microsoft declined to comment [2].

These small parts turn electrical signals into light so that data can travel over fiber-optic cables between servers in a data center [2]. Chinese companies such as Eoptolink and Zhongji Innolight dominate global supply and count the big US cloud groups among their customers [2].

According to Counterpoint Research, Innolight is the world leader with about 27% of this market's revenue, and Chinese manufacturers supply nearly two-thirds of units and about 60% of revenue [3]. Cignal AI even gives it 34% of the sector's revenue in the first quarter of 2026 [4].

The telecoms regulator, the FCC, is preparing the ban: officials fear Beijing could use these parts to steal data or install malware [2]. According to two sources, it would only target models that carry 3.2 terabits per second; the FCC has not said whether or when it will act [2].

Microsoft, which is building 35 data centers in the United States, met in September, along with a handful of other companies, with White House and National Security Council officials to flag supply problems [2]. With other groups, it argues that a ban would slow the data center buildout and weaken the United States against China in AI [2].

The Chinese embassy said it opposes Washington "stretching the concept of national security" to target Chinese companies [2]. A member of the House Select Committee on China, by contrast, supports these restrictions [2].

Key takeaway: America's AI race depends on Chinese parts. Banning these transceivers protects data, but also risks delaying data center projects, as Chinese suppliers account for about 60% of this market [2][3].
It is a new front in the tech rivalry between Washington and Beijing: after chips, the United States is now looking at the components that connect machines to each other [2][5].
For cloud giants, the bill would be immediate: Amazon and Microsoft, big customers of Chinese suppliers, would have to turn to rivals such as Coherent, already well placed in this market [3][5].
For you in France, this tug-of-war could affect the AI and cloud services you use: if data centers cost more or are built more slowly, subscription prices and the rollout of new tools could suffer.

The 2027 budget, rejected by the National Assembly, now goes to the Senate [10].
The Chelles attack changes the mood: the government now speaks of "criminal behaviour", while high school unions condemn the attack without dropping their demands [3][4].

France: the Banque de France now sees only 0.3% growth in 2026, far from the government's 0.5%, and the social crisis clouds the end of the year

On Tuesday 10 November, Banque de France governor Emmanuel Moulin cut his 2026 growth forecast to about 0.3%, from 0.4%, after GDP fell 0.1% in the third quarter. The government, which must find €43 billion in savings, still expects 0.5% [1][2][5][6].
On BFM Business, Emmanuel Moulin explained that the 0.4% estimate was based on positive growth in the third quarter [2]. But GDP fell 0.1% between July and September [1].

"Inevitably, mathematically, it will be very difficult to reach 0.4. So I think we will be rather around 0.3 for the whole year," he said [1]. In early November, he already called that figure "a bit optimistic" and announced a revision in mid-December [3].

He does not expect a new contraction in the fourth quarter [3]. The Banque de France's monthly business survey, published on 9 November and based on about 8,500 companies, forecasts GDP growth of 0.1% to 0.2%, driven mainly by market services [4].
The central bank nevertheless calls the situation "very uncertain", notably because the effect of the social protests on activity remains hard to measure [4].

The government is sticking to its 0.5% forecast, which the High Council of Public Finances considers "hard to achieve" [6]. Emmanuel Moulin said the European Central Bank's next decision on interest rates would come in December [1].

The mechanism is well known: when growth slows, taxes come in more slowly than expected, and the deficit widens unless spending is cut further. A gap between 0.3% and 0.5% therefore makes budget targets harder to meet [5][6].
The timing makes things worse: growth is weakening just as the government must respond to a costly social crisis, for example with a cut in diesel prices promised for at least three months [5].
The relative good news is that the Banque de France sees no recession in the fourth quarter: growth of 0.1% to 0.2% would avoid two consecutive quarters of decline [4][3].

For you, such weak growth means companies cautious about hiring and pay rises, and a state that will look for savings or new revenue in 2027. If you are expecting a pay rise or public support, the budget situation may limit it.
